claim: The Drosophila antennal lobe comprises about 50 distinct glomeruli with stereotyped positions and morphologies.
source: The antennal lobe, the first-order olfactory processing center of Drosophila, comprises about 50 distinct glomeruli with stereotyped positions and morphologies and provides an excellent system for dissecting the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying circuit assembly.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the anatomical structure of the antennal lobe.

claim: Each of the 50 classes of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) expresses a single or a unique set of olfactory receptors.
source: Each of the 50 classes of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) expresses a single or a unique set of olfactory receptors and projects their axons accurately to the 50 corresponding glomeruli in the antennal lobe (Benton et al., 2009; Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Gao et al., 2000; Silbering et al., 2011; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Vosshall et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: ORNs project their axons accurately to the 50 corresponding glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: Each of the 50 classes of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) expresses a single or a unique set of olfactory receptors and projects their axons accurately to the 50 corresponding glomeruli in the antennal lobe (Benton et al., 2009; Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Gao et al., 2000; Silbering et al., 2011; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Vosshall et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Most projection neurons (PNs) arborize their dendrites in a specific glomerulus.
source: Most projection neurons (PNs) arborize their dendrites in a specific glomerulus and form synaptic connections exclusively with the ORNs innervating that glomerulus (Jefferis et al., 2001; Stocker et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PNs form synaptic connections exclusively with the ORNs innervating that glomerulus.
source: Most projection neurons (PNs) arborize their dendrites in a specific glomerulus and form synaptic connections exclusively with the ORNs innervating that glomerulus (Jefferis et al., 2001; Stocker et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plexins are evolutionarily conserved cell-surface receptors that serve as the principal signaling route for semaphorins in the nervous system.
source: Plexins are evolutionarily conserved cell-surface receptors that serve as the principal signaling route for semaphorins in the nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Plexins.

claim: The semaphorin-plexin signaling axis regulates many aspects of neural development, including axon guidance, dendrite targeting, synapse formation, and circuit plasticity.
source: The semaphorin-plexin signaling axis regulates many aspects of neural development, including axon guidance, dendrite targeting, synapse formation, and circuit plasticity (Alto and Terman, 2017; Kolodkin et al., 1993; 1992; Koropouli and Kolodkin, 2014; Kruger et al., 2005; Luo et al., 1993; Meltzer et al., 2016; Orr et al., 2017; Pascoe et al., 2015; Pasterkamp, 2012; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Degenerating larval ORNs build up a gradient of secreted Sema2a and Sema2b: high in the ventromedial (VM) and low in the dorsolateral (DL) antennal lobe.
source: In the developing Drosophila olfactory circuit, degenerating larval ORNs build up a gradient of secreted Sema2a and Sema2b: high in the ventromedial (VM) and low in the dorsolateral (DL) antennal lobe.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of Sema2a and Sema2b in the developing olfactory circuit.

claim: Transmembrane Sema1a forms an opposite gradient and functions cell-autonomously as a receptor to instruct PN dendrite targeting along the VM-DL axis.
source: Transmembrane Sema1a forms an opposite gradient and functions cell-autonomously as a receptor to instruct PN dendrite targeting along the VM-DL axis (Komiyama et al., 2007; Sweeney et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Sema2a/2b gradient determines ORN axon trajectory choice through their canonical receptor PlexB.
source: Moreover, this Sema2a/2b gradient also determines ORN axon trajectory choice through their canonical receptor PlexB (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At about 18 hr after puparium formation (APF), ORN axons arrive at the ventrolateral corner of the antennal lobe and then bifurcate into the DL and VM trajectories.
source: At about 18 hr after puparium formation (APF), ORN axons arrive at the ventrolateral corner of the antennal lobe and then bifurcate into the DL and VM trajectories (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Within 6 hr after arriving at the antennal lobe, ORN axons form two stereotyped bundles circumnavigating the antennal lobe, with a mean DL-to-VM ratio of 0.73.
source: Within the next 6 hr, ORN axons form two stereotyped bundles circumnavigating the antennal lobe, with a mean DL-to-VM ratio of 0.73 (Figure 1A,C) (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,C and a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetic disruption of Sema2b or PlexB biases ORN axons toward the DL trajectory.
source: Genetic disruption of Sema2b or PlexB biases ORN axons toward the DL trajectory, which subsequently leads to incorrect glomerular targeting (Joo et al., 2013), highlighting the significance of this preceding step in the precise assembly of the olfactory map.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetic disruption of Sema2b or PlexB leads to incorrect glomerular targeting.
source: Genetic disruption of Sema2b or PlexB biases ORN axons toward the DL trajectory, which subsequently leads to incorrect glomerular targeting (Joo et al., 2013), highlighting the significance of this preceding step in the precise assembly of the olfactory map.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ORN axons were significantly shifted to the DL trajectory in plexB mutant brains, leading to a mean DL-to-VM ratio of 1.53 in contrast to 0.73 in wild-type brains.
source: Previously, we observed that ORN axons are significantly shifted to the DL trajectory in plexB mutant brains, leading to a mean DL-to-VM ratio of 1.53 in contrast to 0.73 in wild-type brains (Figure 1B,C) (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B,C and a citation.

claim: Supplying PlexB in ORNs largely restores the normal trajectory pattern in plexB mutant flies.
source: Supplying PlexB in ORNs largely restores the normal trajectory pattern in plexB mutant flies, indicating that PlexB functions in ORNs to control the DL versus VM trajectory choice (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PlexB functions in ORNs to control the DL versus VM trajectory choice.
source: Supplying PlexB in ORNs largely restores the normal trajectory pattern in plexB mutant flies, indicating that PlexB functions in ORNs to control the DL versus VM trajectory choice (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and inference from the restoration experiment.

claim: None of the PlexB antibodies could detect the endogenous PlexB signal in developing pupal brains.
source: However, the expression pattern of PlexB remains unknown because none of the PlexB antibodies could detect the endogenous PlexB signal in developing pupal brains (Joo et al., 2013), setting an obstacle for further dissection of its mechanisms of action in axon trajectory choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PlexB-GAL4/plexB– flies were sick and barely survived to adult stage, like plexB–/– homozygotes.
source: Consistently, PlexB-GAL4/plexB– flies were sick and barely survived to adult stage, like plexB–/– homozygotes.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: At 24hAPF, ORN axons circumscribe, but have not innervated, the antennal lobe.
source: At 24hAPF, ORN axons circumscribe, but have not innervated, the antennal lobe, indicating that the signal inside of the antennal lobe was contributed by other types of cells such as PNs, whose dendrites innervate the antennal lobe ahead of ORN axons (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PN dendrites innervate the antennal lobe ahead of ORN axons.
source: At 24hAPF, ORN axons circumscribe, but have not innervated, the antennal lobe, indicating that the signal inside of the antennal lobe was contributed by other types of cells such as PNs, whose dendrites innervate the antennal lobe ahead of ORN axons (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PlexB is transcribed in both DL and VM ORNs.
source: Thus, PlexB is transcribed in both DL and VM ORNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PlexB-GAL4 labeling pattern shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PlexB-GAL4 labeled > 90% of all ORNs.
source: Indeed, by examining the third segments of antennae that house ORN somas, we found that PlexB-GAL4 labeled > 90% of all ORNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Discrepancies between transcription and protein levels due to post-transcriptional and post-translational regulations have been widely reported.
source: Discrepancies between transcription and protein levels due to post-transcriptional and post-translational regulations have been widely reported (Carlyle et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016), necessitating an investigation of the endogenous protein distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The tagged proteins were stably expressed without abnormal degradation and were typically processed.
source: Western blotting of developing pupal brains confirmed that the tagged proteins were stably expressed without abnormal degradation and were typically processed (Artigiani et al., 2003; Ayoob et al., 2006) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: No defects were observed in ORN axon trajectory formation at 24hAPF in either PlexB-Tag/+ or PlexB-Tag/plexB– flies.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any defects in ORN axon trajectory formation at 24hAPF in either PlexB-Tag/+ or PlexB-Tag/plexB– flies, suggesting that the tag does not affect PlexB's functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The tag does not affect PlexB's functions.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any defects in ORN axon trajectory formation at 24hAPF in either PlexB-Tag/+ or PlexB-Tag/plexB– flies, suggesting that the tag does not affect PlexB's functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that PlexB-Tag flies show normal trajectory formation.

claim: Endogenous PlexB proteins may be present at low levels in pupal brains.
source: When performing immunostaining on PlexB-Tag brains using the routine protocol (Wu and Luo, 2006), we detected faint signal that could not consistently generate high-quality images, suggesting that endogenous PlexB proteins may be present at low levels in pupal brains.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of faint signal in immunostaining.

claim: DL axons possessed a higher level of PlexB proteins than VM axons.
source: V5 staining revealed that DL axons indeed possessed a higher level of PlexB proteins (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1L.

claim: PlexB proteins are enriched in DL ORN axons.
source: Consistently, we observed a uniform distribution of PlexB inside the antennal lobe without the edge signals following FLAG staining (Figure 1J), further indicating that PlexB proteins are enriched in DL ORN axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the FLAG staining pattern shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The contrasting patterns between PlexB-GAL4 and PlexB-Tag suggest post-transcriptional or post-translational regulations of PlexB levels.
source: The contrasting patterns between PlexB-GAL4 and PlexB-Tag suggest post-transcriptional or post-translational regulations of PlexB levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observed differences between transcriptional and protein patterns.

claim: PlexB overexpression causes VM ORN axons to shift to the DL trajectory.
source: To test this, we overexpressed PlexB in ORNs and observed that the DL axon bundle was thickened at the expense of the VM bundle (Figure 2A,B), shifting the DL/VM ratio to 1.57 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: PlexB overexpression shifts the DL/VM ratio to 1.57.
source: To test this, we overexpressed PlexB in ORNs and observed that the DL axon bundle was thickened at the expense of the VM bundle (Figure 2A,B), shifting the DL/VM ratio to 1.57 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Elevating the PlexB level drives ORN axons to the DL trajectory in a scalable manner.
source: When the overexpression was intensified by elevating GAL4/UAS-mediated expression at 29°C, the DL shift of ORN axons became more severe (Figure 2C), indicating that elevating the PlexB level drives ORN axons to the DL trajectory in a scalable manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that higher temperature (and thus higher PlexB expression) leads to more severe DL shift.

claim: PlexB overexpression phenotypically resembled loss of PlexB, both of which caused a net VM-to-DL shift of ORN axons.
source: Notably, PlexB overexpression phenotypically resembled loss of PlexB, both of which caused a net VM-to-DL shift of ORN axons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The formation of the VM trajectory requires not only the presence of PlexB but also a specific level of it.
source: This observation indicates that the formation of the VM trajectory requires not only the presence of PlexB but also a specific level of it.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that both loss and overexpression of PlexB cause similar phenotypes.

claim: The PlexB level directs the trajectory choice of ORN axons.
source: In line with the distribution pattern of PlexB proteins (Figure 1L), these findings suggest that the PlexB level directs the trajectory choice of ORN axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the distribution pattern and the effects of PlexB level manipulation.

claim: Axon defasciculation was observed in plexB mutants.
source: In addition to the defect in trajectory choice, we also observed defasciculation of ORN axons in plexB mutants (Figure 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F) (Joo et al., 2013), a phenotype also observed in the development of the embryonic longitudinal tract (Ayoob et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F, and citations.

claim: Axon defasciculation was not observed in PlexB-overexpressing ORNs at either the pupal or the adult stage.
source: However, axon defasciculation was not observed in PlexB-overexpressing ORNs at either the pupal or the adult stage.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of PlexB at a high or low level is sufficient to mediate axon bundling, distinct from its level-dependent effects in trajectory choice.
source: Thus, the presence of PlexB at a high or low level is sufficient to mediate axon bundling, distinct from its level-dependent effects in trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that defasciculation only occurs in plexB mutants but not in PlexB overexpression.

claim: PlexB knockdown drives DL axons to the VM trajectory.
source: When PlexB was knocked down by RNA interference (RNAi) in ORNs, a subset of DA1 ORN axons innervated the VM half of the antennal lobe (red arrow in Figure 2E) while the DL axon bundle was substantially diminished (yellow arrowheads in Figure 2E), indicating that lowering the PlexB level drives DL axons to the VM trajectory.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: A portion of the ectopic VM axons projected back to the DL region and correctly innervated DA1 through a medial entry point.
source: Despite starting with an incorrect trajectory far from their target glomerulus, a portion of the ectopic VM axons projected back to the DL region and correctly innervated DA1 through a medial entry point (red arrowhead in Figure 2E) instead of the original entry points at the edge (yellow arrowheads in Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: The percentage of antennal lobes with ectopic VM axons dropped when PlexB knockdown was performed at higher temperatures.
source: Interestingly, the percentage of antennal lobes with ectopic VM axons dropped when PlexB knockdown was performed at higher temperatures (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2F.

claim: A severe knockdown of PlexB (e.g., at 29°C) resembled the plexB mutant, in which the DL targeting of DA1 axons was caused by the loss of PlexB.
source: Considering the VM-to-DL trajectory shift observed in plexB mutants, it is plausible that a severe knockdown of PlexB (e.g., at 29°C) resembled the plexB mutant, in which the DL targeting of DA1 axons was caused by the loss of PlexB.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed temperature-dependent effects of PlexB knockdown.

claim: All DA1 axons stay DL in plexB mutants.
source: Consistently, all DA1 axons stay DL in plexB mutants (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The VM trajectory requires an intermediate PlexB level.
source: In line with the low level, but not absence, of PlexB proteins in the VM trajectory (Figure 1L), these observations further support the notion that the VM trajectory requires an intermediate PlexB level.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observations of PlexB distribution and the effects of PlexB manipulation.

claim: At 24hAPF, ORN axons form two trajectories circumscribing the antennal lobe before entering it.
source: At 24hAPF, ORN axons form two trajectories circumscribing the antennal lobe before entering it (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: By 48hAPF, the antennal lobe is significantly enlarged and houses proto-glomeruli where the axons and dendrites of matching ORNs and PNs interact.
source: By 48hAPF, the antennal lobe is significantly enlarged and houses proto-glomeruli where the axons and dendrites of matching ORNs and PNs interact (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: PlexB-GAL4 labeled ORN axons of almost every glomerulus at 48hAPF.
source: When intersected with the ORN-specific eyFLP, PlexB-GAL4 labeled ORN axons of almost every glomerulus at 48hAPF (Figure 3C), consistent with the observation that PlexB-GAL4 labeled almost all ORN somas in the antenna (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: PlexB proteins were not uniformly distributed in all ORN axons at 48hAPF.
source: However, PlexB proteins were not uniformly distributed in all ORN axons (Figure 3D), further indicating the presence of post-transcriptional or post-translational regulations of PlexB expression.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Among ORN axons, the ones targeting to the medial glomeruli were the main contributors of PlexB proteins at 48hAPF.
source: Among ORN axons, the ones targeting to the medial glomeruli were the main contributors of PlexB proteins at 48hAPF (Figure 3D), producing a PlexB distribution pattern (medial high and lateral low) distinct from that of 24hAPF (DL high and VM low) through a rapid transition between 30 hr and 36hAPF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Several discrete glomeruli had significantly higher ORN PlexB levels than their neighbors at 48hAPF.
source: Notably, several discrete glomeruli had significantly higher ORN PlexB levels than their neighbors (Figure 3E), including VA4, DM1, and another dorsal glomerulus whose identity could not be unambiguously determined by its position and morphology at 48hAPF.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: The ORN-specific PlexB proteins were highly enriched in the neuropil at 48hAPF.
source: In contrast to concentration in the axons at 24hAPF (Figure 1L), the ORN-specific PlexB proteins were highly enriched in the neuropil at 48hAPF (Figure 3D), where ORN axons meet PN dendrites for partner selection.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: The subcellular localization of PlexB proteins is altered from 24hAPF to 48hAPF.
source: Thus, besides the global change of expression pattern, the subcellular localization of PlexB proteins is also altered from 24hAPF to 48hAPF.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observed differences in PlexB distribution at different developmental stages.

claim: Both overexpression and loss of PlexB drove axons of Or92a+ ORNs to the DL side.
source: Consistent with the previous observations at 24hAPF (Figure 2C), both overexpression and loss of PlexB drove axons of Or92a+ ORNs to the DL side (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B,E.

claim: In the case of AM29+ ORNs, the VM axon bundle disappeared in both PlexB overexpression and loss conditions and likely merged with the original DL track.
source: In the case of AM29+ ORNs, the VM axon bundle disappeared in both conditions and likely merged with the original DL track (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E.

claim: Most ectopic axons innervated ectopic glomeruli in the dorsal half of the antennal lobe.
source: As a consequence, most ectopic axons innervated ectopic glomeruli in the dorsal half of the antennal lobe (Figure 4C,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,F.

claim: The preceding step of trajectory choice largely constrained the possibilities of subsequent glomerular selection by dividing ORN axons into two spatially separated populations.
source: The preceding step of trajectory choice thus largely constrained the possibilities of subsequent glomerular selection by dividing ORN axons into two spatially separated populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that ectopic trajectory choice leads to ectopic glomerular targeting.

claim: ORN axon termini can explore a large area during glomerular selection to partially overcome a prior error in trajectory choice.
source: However, we also observed a small fraction of ectopic axons that ultimately projected back to the VM area (red arrowheads in Figure 4B,E), suggesting that ORN axon termini can explore a large area during glomerular selection to partially overcome a prior error in trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that some ectopic axons can project back to the correct area.

claim: In the PlexB overexpression flies, Or92a+ ORNs mainly targeted to the PlexB-high DM1 glomerulus.
source: In the PlexB overexpression flies, Or92a+ ORNs mainly targeted to the PlexB-high DM1 glomerulus (Figure 4C), while they only chose lateral glomeruli but not DM1 in PlexB knockdown flies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: In PlexB knockdown flies, Or92a+ ORNs only chose lateral glomeruli but not DM1.
source: In the PlexB overexpression flies, Or92a+ ORNs mainly targeted to the PlexB-high DM1 glomerulus (Figure 4C), while they only chose lateral glomeruli but not DM1 in PlexB knockdown flies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4F.

claim: AM29+ ORNs mis-targeted to DM1 when the PlexB level was elevated.
source: Similarly, AM29+ ORNs mis-targeted to DM1 when the PlexB level was elevated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but mis-targeted to DM3 in plexB mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F,G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AM29+ ORNs mis-targeted to DM3 in plexB mutants.
source: Similarly, AM29+ ORNs mis-targeted to DM1 when the PlexB level was elevated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but mis-targeted to DM3 in plexB mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F,G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F,G.

claim: The PlexB level biases glomerular selection when ORNs are forced to ectopically innervate due to incorrect trajectory.
source: Thus, the PlexB level biases glomerular selection when ORNs are forced to ectopically innervate due to incorrect trajectory.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that PlexB level affects glomerular choice in ectopic territory.

claim: PlexB overexpression led to stereotyped mis-targeting of Or92a+ ORNs to the nearby, PlexB-high VA4 glomerulus, along with the loss of VA2 innervation.
source: We found that PlexB overexpression led to stereotyped mis-targeting of Or92a+ ORNs to the nearby, PlexB-high VA4 glomerulus, along with the loss of VA2 innervation (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B,D.

claim: PlexB knockdown caused aberrant targeting around the VA2 area in a small fraction of antennal lobes.
source: PlexB knockdown also caused aberrant targeting around the VA2 area in a small fraction of antennal lobes (Figure 4G), but no innervation to VA4 was observed in the 69 antennal lobes examined.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4G.

claim: No innervation to VA4 was observed in the 69 antennal lobes examined in PlexB knockdown.
source: PlexB knockdown also caused aberrant targeting around the VA2 area in a small fraction of antennal lobes (Figure 4G), but no innervation to VA4 was observed in the 69 antennal lobes examined.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: In more than half of the antennal lobes of PlexB overexpression flies, the AM29+ ORNs had a normal VM axon track but lost DM6 innervation.
source: In more than half of the antennal lobes of PlexB overexpression flies, the AM29+ ORNs had a normal VM axon track but lost DM6 innervation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), which was also observed in a few plexB mutant flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of DM6 innervation was also observed in a few plexB mutant flies.
source: In more than half of the antennal lobes of PlexB overexpression flies, the AM29+ ORNs had a normal VM axon track but lost DM6 innervation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), which was also observed in a few plexB mutant flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The distinct targeting preferences caused by overexpression or loss of PlexB match the endogenous PlexB distribution.
source: Notably, the distinct targeting preferences caused by overexpression or loss of PlexB match the endogenous PlexB distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from comparing the targeting preferences with the endogenous PlexB distribution.

claim: Elevating the PlexB level predominantly drove axons to VA4 or DM1, both of which exhibited high endogenous PlexB levels.
source: Elevating the PlexB level predominantly drove axons to VA4 or DM1, both of which exhibited high endogenous PlexB levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: PlexB knockdown and mutants caused aberrant targeting to DM3 or the lateral glomeruli, whose PlexB levels were low, but not to the PlexB-high glomeruli such as VA4.
source: PlexB knockdown and mutants caused aberrant targeting to DM3 or the lateral glomeruli, whose PlexB levels were low (Figure 3D,E), but not to the PlexB-high glomeruli such as VA4.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D,E.

claim: Independently of its role in trajectory choice, the PlexB level also regulates subsequent glomerular selection in the assembly of the olfactory circuit.
source: Thus, independently of its role in trajectory choice, the PlexB level also regulates subsequent glomerular selection in the assembly of the olfactory circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observations of PlexB level effects on glomerular targeting.

claim: Sema2b is highly enriched in the VM bundle of ORN axons.
source: We previously observed that Sema2b, the canonical ligand of PlexB, is highly enriched in the VM bundle of ORN axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) (Joo et al., 2013), while PlexB proteins are more abundant in DL axons (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and a citation.

claim: Loss of Sema2b causes ORN axons to shift to the DL trajectory.
source: Moreover, loss of Sema2b causes ORN axons to shift to the DL trajectory (Figure 5H) (Joo et al., 2013), similar to PlexB overexpression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5H and a citation.

claim: The phenotypic similarity between loss of Sema2b and PlexB overexpression suggests a potentially antagonistic relationship between Sema2b and PlexB in instructing ORN trajectory choice.
source: Along with the opposing distribution, this phenotypic similarity between loss of Sema2b and PlexB overexpression suggests a potentially antagonistic relationship between Sema2b and PlexB in instructing ORN trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phenotypic similarity and opposing distribution.

claim: sema2b heterozygous flies had normal ORN axon trajectories, indistinguishable from those of wild-type flies.
source: Unlike the homozygotes of the sema2b mutant (Figure 5H), heterozygous flies had normal ORN axon trajectories, indistinguishable from those of wild-type flies (Figure 5A,B,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A,B,E.

claim: The heterozygosity of sema2b significantly promoted the VM-to-DL axon shift caused by elevating the PlexB level.
source: However, the heterozygosity of sema2b significantly promoted the VM-to-DL axon shift caused by elevating the PlexB level (Figure 5C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5C,D,E.

claim: In a subset of sema2b heterozygotes, elevating the PlexB level in ORNs almost completely eliminated the VM trajectory, leading to a single, thick DL bundle.
source: Although PlexB overexpression drove axons to the DL trajectory, the VM bundle was visible in every antennal lobe in a wild-type background (Figure 5C). In a subset of sema2b heterozygotes, however, elevating the PlexB level in ORNs almost completely eliminated the VM trajectory, leading to a single, thick DL bundle (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5D.

claim: sema2b heterozygosity enhanced the VM-to-DL shift of Or92a+ ORN axons caused by PlexB overexpression when examined at the adult stage.
source: In line with this observation at 24hAPF, sema2b heterozygosity also enhanced the VM-to-DL shift of Or92a+ ORN axons caused by PlexB overexpression when examined at the adult stage (Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of one-copy of the Sema2b gene boosts the effect of PlexB overexpression, suggesting that Sema2b partially 'blocks' the effect of high-level PlexB in wild-type flies.

claim: The phenotypic expression of sema2b heterozygosity relied on an elevated PlexB level, suggesting that Sema2b controls ORN axon trajectory choice partly by modulating the level-dependent effects of PlexB.

claim: The combination of PlexB knockdown and sema2b mutant did not drive more axons to the DL bundle; rather, it suppressed the sema2b mutant-induced DL shift.

claim: Sema2b antagonizes the effect of high-level PlexB in glomerular selection.
source: By examining the adult glomerular targeting of Or92a+ and AM29+ ORNs, we observed more antennal lobes with incorrect glomerular innervation when overexpressing PlexB in sema2b heterozygotes (Figure 5L,M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that Sema2b also antagonizes the effect of high-level PlexB in glomerular selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that sema2b heterozygosity enhances PlexB overexpression phenotypes in glomerular targeting.

source: Here, we show that PlexB proteins are distributed at different levels in developing ORN axons, and these patterns change dynamically during development (Figure 1 and Figure 3).

claim: The level of PlexB consecutively controls two critical steps in the assembly of the olfactory map – ORN axon trajectory choice and glomerular selection.
